title: Swipe, Buy, Forget: How the Internet Fragmented Art
excerpt: The digital art market is booming — 18 percent of sales online, Instagram as the gallery, algorithms as curators. But is this really democracy, or just a new form of devaluation?
content:
The Democratization Trap

We've been lying to ourselves. All of us. For years we've been spinning the fairy tale of the democratized art market, of universal equal access, of the end of the elitist white-cube dictatorship. The numbers seem to back us up: 18 percent of global art sales now flow through digital channels, a leap from the meager 13 percent of pre-pandemic times. Platforms are exploding, small galleries find buyers in Seoul who have never set foot in Berlin. A triumph? A little devil.

Because what we're watching isn't emancipation — it's a reshuffling of power. Instead of the grumpy gallerist in a black turtleneck, the algorithm now reigns; instead of the white wall, the bluish screen dominates. Access is there, yes. But access to what? To an endless feed-aesthetic where artworks mutate into content, into scrollable eye-candy wedged between cat videos and ads? When art is everywhere, it is nowhere at all.

The White Cube in Pocket Format

Instagram has reinvented the gallery — new and worse. You used to have to get dressed, step through a door, feel the room. Today you swipe. 51 percent of wealthy collectors now buy digital artworks, ranking them third behind Painting and Sculpture. Gen Z, that mythical creature of every market forecast, is particularly active in digital art, film, and video. They don't collect, they like. They don't curate, they bookmark.

Art Basel caught on early. Its Zero 10 section for digital and New Media art posted sales that left even old hands gawking — a Beeple installation sold out within five hours. What used to require months of diplomatic flirtation now takes a click, a wallet connection, an automated transaction protocol. Faster, more efficient, frozen.

  • Digital platforms democratize market access — but only for those who become visible in the feed
  • Smaller galleries gain new buyers but lose control over the presentation
  • Hybrid models emerge from economic uncertainty, not from artistic vision

The Fragmentation of the Soul

Here it gets meta. Here it gets dangerous. The digital market dismantles the work not only physically but semantically. A painting — a real one, with oil and sweat — is a unity. It breathes as a whole. But in digital space? We buy fragments. We buy crops, JPEGs, video loops. We buy pieces of a whole we'll never lay eyes on, and we fill the gaps with our own meaning.

Imagine an artist breaking his self-portrait into 24,236 single pieces. Each fragment a sliver of his face, his skin, his colors. Abstract, meaningless on its own, only acquiring meaning in the viewer's head. Prices fluctuate between $77 and $777, depending on how much has already sold. The less that's left, the pricier the supposedly special. A game with scarcity, a joke about value. Because in the end the least-loved images will be the most expensive — not because they're beautiful, but because they were left behind. That is the digital market in its purest form: price determines value, not the other way around.

The Algorithm as Curator

And it gets worse. From 2026 on, according to the forecasts, major auction houses will integrate digital pricing signals. Algorithms calculating in real time what a work is "worth." No longer the collector's eye, no longer the gut feeling, no longer the love of color. Just data. Predictive analytics for taste.

The hybrid models currently born of necessity are only a foretaste. They pretend to link online and offline. In truth, they're laying the groundwork for total measurement. When the price becomes transparent, when it becomes calculable, the last shred of magic dies. Then art is definitively a commodity. Then it's nothing but an investment vehicle for the rich who want to get richer, while meaning evaporates like pixels on a dead screen.

I LAUGH YOU

And here we stand. Between $77 and $777, between fragment and whole, between swipe and gaze. The digital revolution hasn't liberated the art market — it has atomized it. It has broken the work into its single pieces, slapped a price tag on every bit, and tossed it into the global current of the attention economy.

But maybe that's exactly where salvation lies. Maybe in this radical fragmentation lies the chance that we wake up. That we grasp: art is not there to be bought. Art is the place where free will expresses itself. It is the bedrock on which meaning — and therefore value — even comes into being in the first place.

If we forget that, if we let algorithms set the price and feeds set the aesthetic, then all that's left is laughter. A bitter, loving, despairing laugh in the face of our own powerlessness. I LAUGH YOU, I then say to the market. Not out of hate. Out of love. Out of the deepest, most wounded love for the art we're all currently optimizing to death.

Because in the end the least-loved fragments will be the most expensive. The joke's on us. Keep swiping.
